law_name: Act No. 659/2007 Coll. on the introduction of the euro in the Slovak Republic (zákon o zavedení meny euro v Slovenskej republike)
description: Framework law adopted on 28 November 2007, during Fico's first government (2006–2010), setting the legal rules for replacing the Slovak koruna with the euro, including the period of dual cash circulation, the exchange of koruna notes and coins and the dual display of prices. Slovakia adopted the euro on 1 January 2009.
significance: Slovakia joined the euro area on 1 January 2009, during the 2008–2009 financial crisis; Fico's government kept the target date for the changeover.

law_name: Act No. 530/2007 Coll. amending Act No. 581/2004 Coll. on health insurance companies (ban on profit distribution)
description: Amendment adopted on 25 October 2007 under Fico's first government requiring health insurance companies to keep separate accounts for public health insurance and to use any positive result from it only for payments for health care, which in effect prevented private insurers from distributing profits from public health insurance to shareholders.
significance: The Dutch insurer Achmea, owner of Union zdravotná poisťovňa, brought an investment arbitration against Slovakia in October 2008; in December 2012 the arbitral tribunal found that Slovakia had breached the Netherlands–Slovakia bilateral investment treaty. Slovakia challenged the award in the German courts, and in 2016 the German Federal Court of Justice referred the question of the treaty's compatibility with EU law to the Court of Justice of the EU, according to TASR.

law_name: Act No. 167/2008 Coll. on periodicals and agency news (tlačový zákon, Press Act)
description: New press law passed on 9 April 2008 by 81 coalition MPs of Fico's first government and in force from 1 June 2008. It introduced a broad right of reply, applicable even where the published information is correct. Fico said the law was modern and secured 'equality of arms' that the old press act lacked.
significance: Publishers and the journalists' syndicate protested and asked the President to veto it, and the opposition linked its support for ratifying the Lisbon Treaty to changes in the bill. The OSCE Representative on Freedom of the Media, Miklós Haraszti, welcomed the removal of a chapter on content restrictions but said on 25 March 2008 that, because his recommendations on the right of reply had not been implemented, the law would still fail to comply with Slovakia's OSCE media-freedom commitments.

law_name: Act No. 318/2009 Coll. amending Act No. 270/1995 Coll. on the State Language of the Slovak Republic
description: Amendment to the State Language Act adopted under Fico's first government and in force from 1 September 2009, whose most criticised part allowed fines of €100 to €5,000 for administrative offences under the act.
significance: The ethnic-Hungarian SMK party considered the fines unconstitutional, and the law strained relations with Hungary; in September 2009 Fico and Hungarian Prime Minister Gordon Bajnai declared that both countries would accept the recommendations of the OSCE High Commissioner on National Minorities, Knut Vollebaek. Vollebaek found several parts compatible with international standards but pointed to terminological shortcomings; on his recommendation the government adopted Principles for the Implementation of the act, effective 1 January 2010, which he welcomed as a safeguard for the linguistic rights of minorities.

law_name: Act No. 395/2012 Coll. amending Act No. 595/2003 Coll. on income tax (end of the flat tax)
description: Amendment passed by parliament in early December 2012 under Fico's single-party second government, ending the flat 19% income tax: from January 2013 monthly income above about €3,300 (176.8 times the subsistence minimum a year) is taxed at 25% instead of 19%, and the corporate income tax rate rose from 19% to 23%; constitutional officials such as MPs and government members pay an additional 5% rate. Fico said those earning €3,300 or more a month should contribute more to consolidating public finances.
significance: Smer argued the measures would help bring the deficit below 3% of GDP in 2013; the Finance Ministry expected €376.6 million in extra revenue that year. The opposition SDKÚ, KDH and Most-Híd criticised the end of the flat tax, a flagship of the previous centre-right reforms, and promised to reintroduce it.

law_name: Act No. 180/2013 Coll. on the organisation of local state administration (ESO reform)
description: Core law of the ESO reform ('Efektívna, spoľahlivá a otvorená štátna správa', efficient, reliable and open state administration) of Fico's second government, led by Interior Minister Robert Kaliňák. From 1 October 2013 it merged the specialised local state administration offices into integrated district offices (okresné úrady) under the Interior Ministry.
significance: Described by the Interior Ministry as the largest reform of state administration since 1989; its first phase had already abolished 64 specialised regional offices. The government presented it as a way to save money and to separate citizens' contact points from the officials who decide their cases.

law_name: Constitutional Act No. 161/2014 Coll. amending the Constitution of the Slovak Republic (marriage; Judicial Council; vetting of judges)
description: Constitutional amendment passed on 4 June 2014 by 102 of the 128 MPs present, with Smer-SD joined by the opposition Christian Democrats (KDH) and a few SDKÚ and OĽaNO MPs, and in force from 1 September 2014. It defines marriage as 'a unique union between a man and a woman', separates the posts of President of the Supreme Court and chair of the Judicial Council, and introduces security clearances (assessment of judicial fitness based in part on information from the state security authority) for judges and judicial candidates.
significance: Fico called its adoption a celebration and said the clearances for judges provided 'a significant ground for cleansing the judiciary'. Human-rights and political-ethics groups protested both its content and the speed of its adoption, and LGBTI activists announced a challenge at the Constitutional Court.

law_name: Action for annulment of the EU Council's September 2015 refugee relocation decision (Slovakia v Council of the EU, Case C-643/15)
description: Policy, not a law: on 2 December 2015 Fico's government filed a lawsuit at the Court of Justice of the EU against the Council decision of September 2015 to relocate 120,000 asylum seekers from Italy and Greece, which had been adopted by majority vote over the opposition of Slovakia, Hungary, the Czech Republic and Romania. Fico called the decision illegitimate; under it Slovakia was to accept 902 people, and according to Interior Minister Kaliňák it had accepted 16 by July 2017.
significance: The Court of Justice dismissed the actions of Slovakia and Hungary on 6 September 2017. Fico said Slovakia respected the court but that its position on quotas remained unchanged.

law_name: Act No. 40/2024 Coll. amending the Criminal Code (Act No. 300/2005) and other laws, including the abolition of the Special Prosecutor's Office
description: Government amendment passed on 8 February 2024 in a fast-track procedure, shortly after Fico's fourth government took office. It abolished the Special Prosecutor's Office (Úrad špeciálnej prokuratúry), which ceased to exist on 20 March 2024, lowered penalties for corruption, property and economic crimes and shortened limitation periods. On 28 February 2024 the Constitutional Court, on petitions by President Zuzana Čaputová and opposition MPs, suspended parts of the law but not the abolition of the Special Prosecutor's Office.
significance: On 17 January 2024 the European Parliament adopted, by 496 votes to 70 with 64 abstentions, a resolution expressing deep concern at the accelerated legislative procedure and the planned dissolution of the Special Prosecutor's Office. In its ruling of 3 July 2024 (PL. ÚS 3/2024) the Constitutional Court upheld most of the law, including the abolition of the office, and found some provisions unconstitutional, among them a transitional rule on limitation, provisions on forfeiture of property and the Justice Minister's power to challenge plea agreements retroactively (as summarised in press reports of the ruling). The restoration of the Special Prosecutor's Office was one of the two questions in the referendum of 4 July 2026, which was invalid because of insufficient turnout.

law_name: Act No. 157/2024 Coll. on Slovak Television and Radio (zákon o Slovenskej televízii a rozhlase, STVR)
description: Law submitted by the Culture Ministry and passed on 20 June 2024 by all 78 MPs present (the opposition did not take part in the vote), in force from 1 July 2024. It replaced Radio and Television of Slovakia (RTVS) with Slovak Television and Radio (STVR) and ended the post of the incumbent RTVS director general on the day it took effect. A nine-member council elects and can dismiss the director general; four members are nominated by the culture minister after a selection procedure and five elected by parliament. It also created a nine-member ethics commission and extended the director general's term from five to six years.
significance: The ministry said the law would depoliticise the election of the broadcaster's leadership and justified the renaming by saying the old name reduced the Slovak nation to a region. Before the vote, media-freedom organisations including the International Press Institute, the Committee to Protect Journalists and the European Broadcasting Union urged parliament to reject the bill, arguing that the appointment of the whole board at once by the parliamentary majority and the culture ministry would give the ruling majority effective control over the board and the director general, contrary to the European Media Freedom Act.

law_name: Act No. 166/2024 Coll. on certain measures to improve the security situation in the Slovak Republic ('lex atentát'), including a lifelong payment for long-serving prime ministers and Speakers
description: Package adopted on 27 June 2024 in a fast-track procedure after the 15 May 2024 assassination attempt on Fico, in force from 15 July 2024. It allows bans on assemblies near the homes of persons whose job or function relates to the assembly's purpose and in residential areas, extends the ban on assemblies to within 50 metres of the seats of the President, the government and general courts, and extends state protection to the Prosecutor General, the President of the Constitutional Court and leaders of parliamentary parties. Amending Act No. 120/1993, it gives a prime minister or Speaker of parliament who has held office for twice the length of a presidential term a lifelong monthly salary; of past office-holders only Fico meets this condition.
significance: Opposition MPs argued the law restricts freedom of assembly and expression and included measures unrelated to the attack, such as the lifelong payment; in February 2025 the Constitutional Court admitted part of their petition for review. Abolishing the lifelong payment was one of the two questions of the referendum of 4 July 2026, which was invalid because of insufficient turnout.

law_name: Act No. 278/2024 Coll. amending laws in connection with further improving the state of public finances (2024 consolidation package)
description: Fiscal consolidation package announced by Fico on 17 September 2024 (about €2.6–2.7 billion, aiming to cut the 2025 deficit to 4.7% of GDP) and adopted in autumn 2024. From 1 January 2025 it raised the standard VAT rate from 20% to 23%, with a reduced 19% rate for most foods and a 5% rate for basic foods, and introduced a 24% corporate income tax rate for companies with taxable income above €5 million. Fico said consolidation was unavoidable because his government had inherited the worst public finances in the EU.
significance: First large tax-raising package of his fourth government, adopted together with the new financial transactions tax and followed by a further package in September 2025.

law_name: Act No. 279/2024 Coll. on the financial transactions tax (zákon o dani z finančných transakcií)
description: Law adopted with the 2024 consolidation package and in force from 1 January 2025, introducing a tax on financial transactions of legal persons and of self-employed natural persons in respect of their business, which must be carried out through a business account: as originally enacted, 0.4% of the transaction amount with a cap of €40 per transaction, and 0.8% on cash withdrawals. When announcing it, Fico said the tax would apply exclusively to legal persons.
significance: In September 2025 parliament rejected an SaS amendment to abolish the tax.

law_name: Act No. 109/2025 Coll. amending Act No. 213/1997 Coll. on non-profit organisations and other laws (the 'NGO law')
description: Coalition law passed on 16 April 2025, signed by President Peter Pellegrini on 7 May 2025 and in force from 1 June 2025. It requires non-governmental non-profit organisations to file transparency reports and disclose donors, places them under oversight by the Interior Ministry and makes those receiving public money subject to the Freedom of Information Act. A provision in earlier drafts labelling NGOs funded from abroad as 'organisations with foreign support' was dropped before the vote. Fico, who had campaigned on 'bringing order' to NGOs, said there was 'nothing Russian' about it.
significance: NGOs and the opposition called it a 'Russian-style law', and the Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights opposed it. On 17 December 2025 the Constitutional Court ruled the law unconstitutional, finding that the public disclosure of donors' identities and donations violated the right to privacy and that treating NGOs as obliged persons under the Freedom of Information Act was disproportionate; the provisions cease to apply once the ruling is published.

law_name: Constitutional Act No. 255/2025 Coll. amending the Constitution of the Slovak Republic (two sexes; national identity in cultural-ethical matters)
description: Constitutional amendment proposed by Fico's government and passed on 26 September 2025 with exactly 90 votes, including some opposition MPs, in force from 1 November 2025. It states that Slovakia recognises only two sexes, male and female, defined by biological criteria; allows adoption only by married couples; bans surrogacy; gives parents the right to decide on their children's participation in education on intimate life and sexual behaviour beyond the state curriculum; guarantees equal pay for women and men; and declares that Slovakia retains sovereignty in matters of national identity, consisting mainly of fundamental cultural-ethical questions such as the protection of life and human dignity, private and family life, marriage, parenthood and family.
significance: Critics said the national-identity clause could conflict with the primacy of EU law. The President cannot veto a constitutional act.

law_name: Act amending laws in connection with the consolidation of public finances (2025 consolidation package for 2026)
description: Main law of the government's consolidation package for 2026, passed in a fast-track procedure on 24 September 2025 by 78 of the 79 MPs present, with the opposition absent from the chamber. It raised taxes and social contributions, moved some foods from the reduced VAT rate to the standard rate, suspended several public holidays as days off in 2026 and froze MPs' salaries for 2026 and 2027 at the 2025 level; according to experts quoted by Pravda, the measures would weigh mainly on employees and the self-employed.
significance: Second large consolidation package of the fourth Fico government, after the 2024 package; associations of small businesses warned of its impact on the self-employed.

law_name: Act on the Office for the Protection of Victims of Crime and Whistleblowers (zákon o Úrade na ochranu obetí trestných činov a oznamovateľov protispoločenskej činnosti), replacing the Whistleblower Protection Office
description: Law drafted by the Interior Ministry, approved by the government in November 2025 and passed by 78 coalition MPs on 9 December 2025 in a fast-track procedure; parliament then overrode President Pellegrini's veto. It would have transformed the Whistleblower Protection Office (ÚOO) into a new office that would also take over compensation of crime victims from the Justice Ministry; the opposition objected among other things to the shortening of the term of the ÚOO's elected head and to the possibility of reviewing protection already granted to whistleblowers.
significance: On 17 December 2025 the Constitutional Court suspended the law before it took effect and admitted the opposition's petition in full; the Ombudsman supported the petition. Because the European Commission had suspended the assessment of Slovakia's Recovery and Resilience Facility payment requests while the law was valid, the coalition repealed it in full on 17 March 2026 through an amendment attached to a Criminal Code bill, signed by the President on 23 March 2026, so the ÚOO continues to operate.

law_name: Civil Code of 1 October 2026 (Občiansky zákonník), new codification of private law
description: Government bill of Justice Minister Boris Susko, drafted by a codification commission of judges, notaries, lawyers and law professors chaired by Professor Marek Števček, passed by the National Council on 1 October 2026 with 90 votes and signed by President Pellegrini on 20 October 2026. It replaces the Civil Code of 1964, amended about 70 times since 1991, ends the dual regime of civil and commercial contract law in favour of a single set of rules, and widens contractual freedom while keeping consumer protection and the basic concept of spouses' joint property.
significance: The first new basic code of private law in Slovakia in more than 60 years; Susko said it was meant to be a modern code prepared by experts rather than a political project.
